modules.title: Meet BFS
goals: Explain what BFS is for, and when it is the right tool.
Trace BFS by hand: say which vertex comes next, what is in the queue, which vertices are visited and the order they are visited in.
Use BFS to find the route with the fewest edges between two places, and say why BFS guarantees it.

segments.title: Why BFS? The fewest walkways
segments.body:
It's your first day on campus. You're at the Admin block, A, and your friends are waiting at the Green, G. You want the route with the fewest walkways. How would you find it?

```
   A ─── C ─── B ─── G
   │     │
   E ─── F
   │
   D
```

A Admin block · B Bookshop · C Computer Science building · D Dining hall · E Engineering building · F Fountain · G Green (sports field)

The walkways are A–C, A–E, B–C, B–G, C–F, D–E and E–F.

Each place is a vertex, and each walkway is an edge. The walkways go both ways, so this is an undirected graph, just like in module 1.

One way to search is in rings. First, every building one walkway from A: that is A's neighbours, C and E. Then every building two walkways away: B, F and D. Then three: G. The first time you reach G, you know you've used the fewest walkways possible.

Searching ring by ring like this is called **breadth-first search**, or BFS. "Breadth-first" means we go wide before we go deep: we finish one ring before we start the next.

BFS is useful whenever you care about the fewest steps: fewest stops on a train map, friends of friends on a social network, or the fewest moves in a puzzle.

Next, you'll see how BFS keeps track of the rings, using something you already know: a queue.

segments.title: When is BFS the right tool?
Worked example: is BFS the right tool?
segments.body:
Is BFS the right tool? Ask two questions.

**Question 1. Is there a graph?** Are there things joined to other things? If not, there is nothing for BFS to search.

**Question 2. What does the problem ask for?** BFS reaches vertices in rings: first everything one edge from the start, then everything two edges away, and so on. So it is the right tool for **the fewest edges** to somewhere, or **everything within a number of edges** of a start. It counts edges, so it is not the right tool when each edge has its own length or cost.

| Problem | 1. A graph? | 2. What is asked? | BFS? |
|---|---|---|---|
| The fewest clicks from one web page to another | Yes: pages joined by links | The fewest edges | Good fit |
| The quickest drive, when each road takes a different number of minutes | Yes: places joined by roads | The least total time, not the fewest roads | Not a fit |
| The highest mark in a test | No: the marks aren't joined | – | Not a fit |

**Explain it to yourself before you go on:** a drive along more roads can still be quicker. Why does that rule BFS out for the quickest drive?

segments.title: Try another: is BFS the right tool?
BFS step by step on the campus
segments.body:
To search ring by ring, BFS needs to remember which buildings are waiting to be explored. It uses a **queue**: first in, first out, like the line at the dining hall.

Two words matter here. A vertex is **found** when it joins the queue, and BFS never adds a vertex it has already found. It is **visited** when it leaves the queue, which is when it joins the order. Joining the queue is also called being **enqueued**, and leaving it being **dequeued**.

We start by putting A in the queue. A is now found: BFS will never add it to the queue again.

BFS repeats three steps until the queue is empty:

1. Take the vertex at the front of the queue. It is now **visited**.
2. Add it to the order.
3. Add each of its neighbours that hasn't been found yet to the back of the queue. Take the neighbours in alphabetical order.

**A leaves.** A is visited. Its neighbours are C and E. Neither has been found yet, so both join the queue. The queue is now C, E.

**C leaves.** The queue holds C, then E, so BFS takes C: it joined first, so it leaves first. C's neighbours are A, B and F. A has already been found, so we skip it. B and F join at the **back**, behind E. The queue is now E, B, F.

**E leaves.** E is at the front now. Its neighbours are A, D and F. A is visited. D is new. But what about F? F hasn't been visited yet: it is still waiting in the queue. So F is skipped. It was found when it joined the queue, so it can't be added a second time, even though it hasn't been visited yet. Only D joins. The queue is now B, F, D. That is why BFS checks whether a vertex has been *found*, not only whether it has been visited.

**B leaves.** Its new neighbour is G, so G joins the back of the queue. The queue is now F, D, G.

**F, D and G leave** in turn. All of their neighbours have already been found, so nothing new joins. The queue is empty, and BFS is finished.

The order is **A, C, E, B, F, D, G**. Look at the rings: first A, then the one-walkway buildings C and E, then B, F and D, and finally G. The queue is what keeps the rings in order.

Now it's your turn. In the visualiser you'll predict every step before it happens.

segments.title: Your turn: predict every step
segments.body:
Open the BFS visualiser on the campus graph: **[predict every step](/graphs/4)**.

Before each step, pick the vertex BFS takes next.

- Look at the queue panel, not the graph: BFS always takes the vertex at the **front** of the queue.
- Alphabetical order only decides the order neighbours **join** the queue, not which vertex leaves next.
- A vertex that hasn't joined the queue yet can't be next.

segments.title: Worked example: filling in a trace table
segments.body:
We trace BFS on the campus graph from **A**, one row for each vertex that leaves the queue. A vertex is **found** when it joins the queue, and BFS never adds a vertex it has already found. It is **visited** when it leaves the queue, which is when it joins the order.

Every row follows the same four subgoals. First, **initialise**: the start is found and waits in the queue (the start row). Then, for each row: **take the next vertex** from the front of the queue. Then, **for each neighbour** of that vertex, in alphabetical order, ask whether it has been found. If it hasn't, **mark and enqueue** it: it is found and joins the back.

| Step | Current vertex | Queue after the step | Visited | Order so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | A | – | – |
| 1 | A | C, E | A | A |
| 2 | C | E, B, F | A, C | A, C |
| 3 | E | B, F, D | A, C, E | A, C, E |

**Step 1.** *Take the next vertex:* A leaves the queue, so it is visited and joins the order. *For each neighbour:* A's neighbours in alphabetical order are C and E. *Mark and enqueue:* neither has been found yet, so both join the back of the queue.

**Step 2.** *Take the next vertex:* C is at the front, so C leaves. *For each neighbour:* its neighbours are A, B and F. *Mark and enqueue:* A has been found already, so only B and F join.

**Step 3.** *Take the next vertex:* E leaves. *For each neighbour:* its neighbours are A, D and F. *Mark and enqueue:* A is visited, and F is already waiting in the queue, so only D joins.

The remaining steps work the same way. The full order is **A, C, E, B, F, D, G**.

segments.title: Worked example: a vertex that is already waiting
segments.body:
Here is a whole trace on a new graph, with one tricky step. The graph is undirected, with vertices M, N, P, Q, R and S, and edges M–S, N–Q, N–R, P–R, Q–S and R–S. We start at **Q**. A vertex is **found** when it joins the queue, and **visited** when it leaves.

| Step | Current vertex | Queue after the step | Visited | Order so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | Q | – | – |
| 1 | Q | N, S | Q | Q |
| 2 | N | S, R | Q, N | Q, N |
| 3 | S | R, M | Q, N, S | Q, N, S |
| 4 | R | M, P | Q, N, S, R | Q, N, S, R |
| 5 | M | P | Q, N, S, R, M | Q, N, S, R, M |
| 6 | P | (empty) | Q, N, S, R, M, P | Q, N, S, R, M, P |

**The hard step is step 3.** S leaves the queue. Its neighbours, in alphabetical order, are M, Q and R. Q is visited already. R hasn't been visited, but it is **already waiting** in the queue: it was found at step 2, so it doesn't join again. Only M is new, so only M joins the back.

**For each row, ask two questions.** Which vertex is at the front? It leaves and is visited. Which of its neighbours haven't been found yet? Those join the back, in alphabetical order.

**Explain it to yourself before you go on:** at step 4, R leaves, and its neighbours are N, P and S. Why does only P join the queue?

segments.title: Worked example: the fewest walkways, and why BFS finds them
segments.body:
**Worked example.** BFS from the Admin block (A) on the campus graph visits A, C, E, B, F, D, G. Each time a vertex joins the queue, write down **who found it**:

| Vertex | Found by | Walkways from A |
|---|---|---|
| A | (the start) | 0 |
| C | A | 1 |
| E | A | 1 |
| B | C | 2 |
| F | C | 2 |
| D | E | 2 |
| G | B | 3 |

**Step 1. Start at the goal and walk back.** Who found D? E. Who found E? A. So the route is A → E → D: **2 walkways**.

**Step 2. Why there is no shorter route.** BFS takes vertices out of the queue ring by ring: everything 1 walkway from A, then everything 2 away, then 3. D was found while BFS worked through the 1-walkway ring, so D is 2 away. If D were 1 away, A itself would have found it.

**The rule:** when every edge counts the same, the first time BFS reaches a vertex is by the **fewest edges**, and following "found by" back to the start gives that route. (When edges have their own lengths, such as kilometres, the fewest edges may not be the shortest distance: that needs another algorithm.)

segments.title: Worked example: walking back from the goal
segments.body:
Here is the "found by" method again, on a small new graph. The edges are Q–R, Q–S, R–T, S–T and T–U, and BFS starts at Q.

| Vertex | Found by | Edges from Q |
|---|---|---|
| Q | (the start) | 0 |
| R | Q | 1 |
| S | Q | 1 |
| T | R | 2 |
| U | T | 3 |

T is found by R, not S, because R leaves the queue first. **Walk back from U:** T, then R, then Q. The route Q → R → T → U has **3 edges**.

**Two mistakes to avoid.** Count the **edges** (the steps between vertices), not the vertices on the route: Q, R, T, U is 4 vertices but 3 edges. And don't count how far a vertex is along the visit order: U is 5th in the order, but only 3 edges from Q.

**Explain it to yourself before you go on:** why does R find T, and not S?

config.prompt: The walkways on campus can be used in both directions. What kind of graph is the campus map?

options.label: It is not a graph, because walkways have different lengths

solution.explanation: A walkway can be used both ways, so its edge has no direction: the graph is undirected. Lengths don't change whether it is a graph.

feedback.b: Not quite. A directed edge only goes one way, like a one-way street. These walkways go both ways. Ask: can every walkway be used in both directions?
feedback.c: Not quite. Edges can have lengths (weights) and still be a graph. Here we only care whether two buildings are connected. Ask: are there things joined by connections?

hints.body: Think back to module 1: what is the difference between a directed and an undirected edge?
A directed edge has an arrow and can only be followed one way.
Can you walk from A to C and also from C to A? Then the edge has no single direction.
Answer: an undirected graph, because every walkway can be used in both directions.

activities.title: Quick recall: a graph in Python

config.prompt: Using the Graph class from module 2, an empty undirected graph runs add_vertex("A"), add_vertex("C") and then add_edge("A", "C"). What is adjacency now?

solution.explanation: In an undirected graph add_edge connects both ways, so A gets C as a neighbour and C gets A.

feedback.b: Not quite. That is a directed edge from A to C. In an undirected graph C must also list A. Check C's list.
feedback.c: Not quite. Each vertex maps to a list of neighbours, and both A and C are in the dictionary. Look for a list on both sides.

hints.body: Remember how module 2 stored an undirected edge.
Each vertex has a list of its neighbours.
If A is a neighbour of C, then C is also a neighbour of A.
Answer: {"A": ["C"], "C": ["A"]}: the edge is stored once in each vertex's list.

activities.title: When is BFS the right tool?

config.prompt: For each situation, choose whether BFS is a good fit and why. A reason can fit more than one situation, and some reasons fit none.

left.label: Find the route between two stations on the Gautrain map with the fewest stops.
List everyone who is a friend, or a friend of a friend, of Thandi on a social network.
Add up the prices of all items in a shopping list.
Find the fewest links you must click to get from one web page to another.
Find the route between two Gautrain stations with the shortest travel time.

right.label: Good fit: BFS explores one ring of neighbours at a time, so it finds all the vertices close to the start first.
Good fit: BFS takes neighbours in alphabetical order, so it lists the items in order.
Not a fit: BFS counts edges, but here the edges aren't all worth the same.
Not a fit: there are no connections to follow, so this is not a graph problem.
Good fit: BFS works outwards one edge at a time, so it first reaches the goal by a shortest path.
Not a fit: BFS follows paths on a map, so it can't follow links between people.

solution.explanation: BFS fits when there are connections to follow and you want the fewest edges, or everyone within a few edges. Adding up prices has no connections, and the quickest trip depends on each edge's time, not on how many edges there are.

feedback.s1: Not quite. Each stop-to-stop ride is an edge, so the fewest stops is the fewest edges. Look for the reason about how BFS reaches vertices ring by ring.
feedback.s2: Not quite. Friends are one edge away and friends of friends two. BFS finds them ring by ring, whatever the vertices stand for. Look for the reason about rings of neighbours.
feedback.s3: Not quite. A list of prices has no vertices and edges to traverse, so a simple loop is enough. Look for the reason that says there is nothing to follow.
feedback.s4: Not quite. Pages are vertices and links are edges, so the fewest clicks is the fewest edges. Alphabetical order only decides which neighbour joins the queue first. Look for the reason about how BFS reaches vertices ring by ring.
feedback.s5: Not quite. Each ride between stations takes its own time, so the route with the fewest stops isn't always the quickest. BFS counts edges, not minutes. Look for the reason about edges that aren't all worth the same.

hints.body: First ask: are there things connected to other things? If not, it is not a graph problem.
BFS explores everything one edge away, then everything two edges away, and so on.
'Fewest stops', 'fewest clicks' and 'friend of a friend' are all about counting edges from a start. Any connections can be edges, not only paths on a map. Travel time is not a count of edges.
Answer: s1 → r1 (fewest stops), s2 → r2 (ring by ring), s3 → r3 (not a graph), s4 → r1 (fewest clicks), s5 → r6 (edges not all worth the same).

config.prompt: The campus graph has the walkways A–C, A–E, B–C, B–G, C–F, D–E and E–F. BFS starts at A and takes neighbours in alphabetical order. After C is processed, what is in the queue (front first)?

solution.explanation: After A, the queue was C, E. Processing C takes it from the front and adds its new neighbours, B and F, at the back, so the queue is E, B, F.

feedback.b: E was already waiting. New vertices join at the back, so E stays in front.
feedback.c: B and F join together at the back, after E.
feedback.d: C left the front of the queue when it was processed, so it isn't in the queue any more.

config.prompt: Which of these is not a job for BFS?

options.label: Find the route between two stations on the Gautrain map with the fewest stops.
List everyone who is a friend, or a friend of a friend, of Thandi on a social network.
Add up the prices of all items in a shopping list.
Find the fewest links you must click to get from one web page to another.

solution.explanation: BFS follows connections, ring by ring from the start. A list of prices has no connections to follow, so a simple loop adds them up. The other three are graphs where you want the fewest steps, or everyone within a few steps.

feedback.a: Fewest stops means fewest edges, the order in which BFS reaches vertices.
feedback.b: Friends are one edge away and friends of friends two. BFS finds them ring by ring.
feedback.d: Pages are vertices and links are edges, so the fewest clicks is the fewest edges.

config.prompt: BFS starts at A on the undirected graph with edges A–B, A–D, B–C, C–E and D–E, taking neighbours in alphabetical order. In what order does it visit the vertices?

solution.explanation: A's neighbours B and D join the queue first. Then B adds C, and D adds E. So the order is A, B, D, C, E: everything one edge from A before anything two edges away.

feedback.a: That goes deep first. BFS visits both of A's neighbours, B and D, before C.
feedback.b: That is alphabetical order. BFS visits by distance from A: D is one edge away, C two.
feedback.d: Neighbours are taken in alphabetical order, so B joins the queue before D.

config.prompt: An undirected graph has the edges D–E, D–G, E–H, G–K, G–L, H–L and K–L. What is the fewest number of edges from D to L?

solution.explanation: BFS from D finds E and G at one edge, then H, K and L at two: G finds L. BFS reaches each vertex by a route with the fewest edges, so two is the fewest.

feedback.a: No edge joins D to L: D's only neighbours are E and G. Count the rings BFS finds from D.
feedback.c: D–E–H–L is a route, but there is a shorter one: G is joined to L. Count the rings BFS finds from D.
feedback.d: 7 is the number of edges in the whole graph. Count only the edges on one route.

config.prompt: In step 3 of the worked example, E leaves the queue. Its neighbours are A, D and F, but only D joins. Why doesn't F join the queue?

options.label: F was found at step 2 and is already waiting in the queue.
F comes after D in the alphabet, so it must wait its turn.
F has been visited already, so it is in the order so far.

solution.explanation: C added F at step 2, so F has been found and is waiting in the queue. BFS never adds a vertex it has already found, so F doesn't join a second time.

feedback.b: Not quite. Alphabetical order only decides the order in which new neighbours join. F is left out because C already added it at step 2. Before a neighbour joins, check whether it is already in the queue.
feedback.c: Not quite. F isn't in the order yet: it is still waiting in the queue, so it is found but not visited. BFS adds only neighbours it hasn't found, so check the queue as well as the order.

hints.body: Look at the queue after step 2.
After step 2 the queue is E, B, F.
F joined at step 2, when C left. Can a vertex be in the queue twice?
Answer: F was found at step 2 and is already waiting in the queue.

activities.title: Trace BFS from B: one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

solution.explanation: BFS takes the vertex at the front of the queue and adds its neighbours not found yet, in alphabetical order, at the back. B finds A and D, then A finds C. When D leaves, C is already waiting in the queue, so it isn't added again, and C then finds E.

hints.body: Start with only B in the queue. Nothing is visited yet. Row 1 is what happens when B leaves.
For each row: take the vertex at the front of the queue. It is now visited and joins the order. Then add its neighbours that haven't been found yet, in alphabetical order, at the back of the queue.
Row 1: B leaves, and its neighbours A and D join. Row 2: A leaves. Its neighbours are B and C, and only C is new.
Answer: the order is B, A, D, C, E. The queue after each row is [A, D], [D, C], [C], [E], []. At row 3, C is not added again because it is already waiting in the queue.

config.prompt: Closing task. BFS now starts at the Engineering building (E) on the campus graph (walkways A–C, A–E, B–C, B–G, C–F, D–E, E–F). It records who found each building. Walk back from the Bookshop (B) along those records: what route do you get, and how many walkways long is it?

solution.explanation: Correct. E finds A, D and F. A leaves the queue before F, so A finds C first, and C finds B. Walking back from B gives E → A → C → B: 3 walkways. BFS takes every building 2 walkways from E out of the queue before any 3 away, so no route is shorter.

feedback.f: Not quite. E → F → C → B is also 3 walkways, but it isn't the route BFS records. A and F both neighbour C, and A leaves the queue first, so A finds C. Ask: who took C into the queue?
feedback.g: Not quite. There's no walkway between E and C: E's neighbours are A, D and F. Check E's walkways in the list, then walk back from B.
feedback.h: Not quite. The route is right, but 4 counts the buildings E, A, C and B. Each walkway joins two of them, so there is one fewer walkway than buildings. Count the arrows.

hints.body: Run BFS from E and write down who found each building.
E finds A, D and F, in that order. Which of A and F leaves the queue first?
A leaves first, so A finds C. Who finds B?
Answer: E → A → C → B, 3 walkways.

activities.title: Try another: trace BFS from F, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

solution.explanation: BFS takes the vertex at the front of the queue and adds its neighbours not found yet, in alphabetical order, at the back. F finds D and H, then D finds E. When H leaves, E and F have both been found already, so nothing joins, and E then finds G.

hints.body: Start with only F in the queue. Nothing is visited yet. Row 1 is what happens when F leaves.
For each row: the vertex at the front leaves and is visited. Its neighbours that haven't been found yet join the back, in alphabetical order.
Row 1: F leaves, and D and H join. Row 2: D leaves. Its neighbours are E and F, and only E is new. Row 3: H leaves. E is already waiting in the queue, so nothing joins.
Answer: the order is F, D, H, E, G. The queue after each row is [D, H], [H, E], [E], [G], [].

activities.title: Try another: is BFS the right tool?

config.prompt: For each problem, choose whether BFS is a good fit and why.

left.label: Find the fewest moves a chess knight needs to get from one square of the board to another.
In a video game, find every room of a castle that is no more than two doors from the entrance.
Plan the trip between two towns that uses the least petrol, when every road uses a different amount.
Count how many learners in a class wrote the test.

right.label: Not a fit: BFS counts edges, but here each edge has its own length or cost.
Good fit: the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has used as few edges as possible.
Good fit: BFS follows one path as far as it goes, so it finds the longest route.
Not a fit: nothing is joined to anything, so there is no graph to search.
Good fit: BFS has found everything one edge away before it finds anything two edges away.

solution.explanation: BFS reaches everything one edge away before anything two edges away, so the first route it finds uses the fewest edges: that fits the knight's moves and the rooms within two doors. It counts edges, not what each one costs, so it can't find the trip with the least petrol, and counting learners has no edges to follow at all.

feedback.s1: Not quite. The squares are vertices and each knight move is an edge, so the fewest moves is the fewest edges from the start. Look for the reason about the fewest edges.
feedback.s2: Not quite. The rooms are vertices and the doors are edges, and no more than two doors means everything within two edges. Look for the reason about finding everything one edge away first.
feedback.s3: Not quite. There is a graph, but each road uses its own amount of petrol, and BFS only counts edges: a trip along more roads can still use less petrol. Look for the reason about each edge having its own length.
feedback.s4: Not quite. Counting learners needs no connections between them, so there is no graph and nothing for BFS to search. Look for the reason that says there is no graph.

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined to other things? If not, there is no graph.
Then ask what the problem wants: the fewest edges, everything within some number of edges, or the least total length?
BFS counts edges and works ring by ring, so it ignores lengths and costs. It doesn't follow one path to its end first.
Answer: knight → the fewest edges; castle rooms → everything one edge away before two; least petrol → each edge has its own length; counting learners → no graph to search.

config.prompt: BFS now starts at the Fountain (F) on the campus graph (edges A–C, A–E, B–C, B–G, C–F, D–E, E–F) and visits F, C, E, A, B, D, G. What is the fewest number of walkways from F to the Green (G)?

solution.explanation: Walking back from G: B found G, C found B, and F found C. The route F → C → B → G has 3 walkways, and BFS guarantees none is shorter.

feedback.a: Not quite. No walkway joins C to G. Walk back from G: B found G, C found B, F found C. That is 3 walkways. Count each step back.
feedback.c: Not quite. 4 is the number of places on the route F, C, B, G, not the walkways between them. Count the edges, not the vertices.

hints.body: Write down who found each vertex as BFS runs from F.
F found C and E; C found A and B. Who found G?
B found G. Now walk back from G to F and count the steps.
Answer: 3 walkways, F → C → B → G.

config.prompt: In a small network, H links to J and K, both J and K link to L, and L links to M. Starting BFS at H, how many edges lie on the shortest route to M?

solution.explanation: BFS from H finds J and K (1 edge away), then L (2), then M (3). The route H → J → L → M has 3 edges.

feedback.a: Not quite. M links only to L, and L is 2 edges from H, so M is one more. Ask: who found M, and who found that vertex?
feedback.b: Not quite. 5 is M's place in the visit order H, J, K, L, M, not how many edges away it is. Walk back from M and count the edges.
feedback.c: Not quite. 4 is the number of vertices on the route H, J, L, M. The edges between them are one fewer, so count the edges.

hints.body: Who found J and K? Who found L?
J found L. Who found M?
L found M. Walk back: M, L, J, H.
Answer: 3 edges, H → J → L → M.

config.prompt: Optional bonus quest. The walkway between the Bookshop (B) and Computer Science (C) is closed for repairs. The walkways still open are A–C, A–E, B–G, C–F, D–E and E–F. You run BFS from the Admin block (A). Which places can it no longer reach?

options.label: None: BFS still reaches every place
The Dining hall (D) and the Engineering building (E)

solution.explanation: BFS from A reaches C and E, then F and D. With B–C closed, B and G are joined only to each other, so nothing BFS reaches leads to them: they are a separate piece of the graph.

feedback.b: Not quite. The Green's only walkway goes to the Bookshop, so once B can't be reached, G can't be either. Check G's walkways too.
feedback.c: Not quite. With B–C closed, the Bookshop's only walkway goes to the Green, and the Green's only one goes back to the Bookshop. List what BFS reaches from A and see whether any of it leads to them.
feedback.d: Not quite. A–E is still open, and D–E leads on to the Dining hall, so BFS reaches E and D in its first two rings. Look for places with no open walkway to anything BFS reaches.

hints.body: List what BFS from A can reach, ring by ring.
Ring 1: C and E. Ring 2: F and D. Does any of them have an open walkway to B or G?
With B–C closed, B's only walkway goes to G, and G's only one goes to B. Nothing BFS reaches leads to either.
Answer: the Bookshop (B) and the Green (G).
